check.q: Why does the Spice Guard test have a square with plain rice flour on top?
options: To check whether any powder at all stops mould, or only the spice
To make the potato taste better
Because rice flour is a strong medicine
check.why: Rice flour is a dry powder like haldi and clove, but it has no strong chemical. If the rice flour square also stays clean, the powder layer was doing the work. If it grows mould, the spice chemical made the difference.

flow.do: 1. Close each box tightly. 2. Draw a 4 by 4 grid of squares on each lid with the marker, over the potato. 3. Put all four boxes together in a cupboard away from the stove.
flow.say: The grid gives us 16 small squares on each potato. Each day we count how many have mould. Counting turns what we see into numbers we can compare.
flow.kid: Close the boxes. Draw a grid of 16 squares on each lid. Put them in a cupboard together.
flow.parent: Mould grows faster in warm, damp weather. A cupboard that stays warm, like one near the fridge, is good. Not next to the stove.

flow.do: Each day from day 2 to day 7, take out the boxes without opening them. Count the grid squares on each lid that have mould under them. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: Look closely through the lid. Mould starts as white fuzz, then may turn green, grey or black. Slimy wet patches count too. How many squares have some?
flow.kid: Look through each lid. Count the squares with fuzz or slime. Write the number. Do not open the box.
flow.parent: In warm weather, mould often shows on the plain and rice flour squares by day 3 to 5. The clove square usually stays clean or nearly clean all week. Haldi often slows the mould but may not stop them. In cold weather, keep counting up to day 10.

flow.do: Help your child draw a line graph. The bottom line shows the days, from 2 to 7. The side shows squares with mould, from 0 to 16. Draw one line for each potato, in four colours.
flow.say: Each potato gets their own line. Watch the lines. Which line climbs fastest? Which stays flat?
flow.kid: Draw a line for each potato. Days go along the bottom. Mould squares go up the side.

check.q: Suppose that in Spice Guard the rice flour square grows as much mould as the plain square. What does this show?
options: A plain powder does not protect the potato, so any protection came from the spice's chemical
Rice flour is a medicine
Mould cannot grow on potato
check.why: Rice flour is a powder too, but it gave no protection. So a square that stayed clean, like the clove square, was protected by the chemical in the spice, not by being covered.

flow.do: Ask your child for three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened. Then read the explanation card 'A plant's shield, borrowed by us'.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A strong answer sounds like this. What I think: clove stops mould, and haldi slows the mould a little. What I saw: by day 6 the plain square had 12 mouldy squares, rice flour had 13, haldi had 5 and clove had 0. Why: cloves have a strong chemical that protects the bud from moulds. Accept your own family's real numbers, even if they differ.

flow.do: A grown-up throws the closed boxes or bags straight into the bin. If you want to keep the boxes, empty them into the bin outdoors and wash them in hot soapy water.
flow.say: We never open the boxes near our faces. The mould is still alive and making spores.
flow.kid: A grown-up throws the boxes away. Wash your hands.

experiments.title: The Node Test: which money plant cuttings grow roots?
experiments.question: Does a money plant cutting need a node, or a leaf, to grow new roots?
experiments.predict: You will put three pieces of money plant stem in water: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node but no leaf, and one with no node at all. Which will grow roots first? Will any grow no roots? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is about 3 cm long, and the bottom 2 cm of each stands in water, so the node of A and B is under water. All three stand in the same kind of glass, with the same depth of water, by the same window. Only the node and the leaf change. Change the water in all three glasses on the same days.

materials.item: a healthy money plant, your own or a neighbour's. A small pot from a nursery costs very little
clean scissors, used by a grown-up
3 small glasses or clear plastic bottles cut in half
tap water, left in a jug overnight
a ruler with millimetres
a marker or paper labels and tape

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Money plant sap can irritate skin and is harmful if eaten, so wash your hands after handling the cuttings, and keep cuttings away from small children and pets.

schedule.what: Find the nodes. Cut three pieces. Put them in water by a bright window. Guess.
Count the roots on each cutting and measure the longest one in millimetres. Change the water.
Count and measure again. Change the water.
Count and measure again. Change the water.
Last count and measurement. Draw a bar chart of the longest root on each cutting. Plant the rooted cutting in soil.

experiments.record: Write the number of roots and the length of the longest root for each cutting on days 4, 7, 10 and 14. On day 14, draw a bar chart of the longest roots.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out which part of a stem can grow new roots, by testing three money plant cuttings in water.

setup.art: A money plant stem with arrows pointing to the nodes, where each leaf joins the stem, and the small brown bump at each node.
setup.caption: 1. Find the nodes, where leaves join the stem.

setup.art: Three short stem pieces on a plate: A with a node and a leaf, B with a node but the leaf cut off, C a bare piece from between two nodes.
setup.caption: 2. Cut three pieces: A, B and C.

setup.art: Three labelled glasses of water on a bright windowsill, each with one cutting, the bottom 2 cm under water.
setup.caption: 3. Stand each in water by a bright window.

setup.art: A ruler held beside white roots growing out of the node of cutting A in a glass.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the longest root in millimetres.

flow.do: Look at the money plant together. Find where each leaf joins the stem. Point out the small brown bump there.
flow.say: This place where the leaf joins the stem is called a node. The bump is a root waiting to grow. What do you think the bare stem between two nodes can do?
flow.kid: Find where a leaf joins the stem. That is a node. Can you see the little bump?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Node Test. You find out which pieces of stem can grow roots.

flow.do: 1. Cut piece A. Cut about 1 cm below a node and about 2 cm above it. The piece is 3 cm long, with the node near the bottom and its leaf still on. 2. Cut piece B the same way from another node, then snip off the leaf. 3. Cut piece C: 3 cm of bare stem from between two nodes, with no node.
flow.say: Each piece has the same length of stem. Only the node and the leaf are different. Why does that make the test fair?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts three pieces. A has a node and a leaf. B has a node but no leaf. C has no node.
flow.parent: On small indoor plants the bare stem between nodes can be short. Cut C as long as you can, even 2 cm is fine, and cut A and B to the same length as C.

flow.do: 1. Label three glasses A, B and C. 2. Pour the same amount of water into each. 3. Stand each piece so the bottom 2 cm is under water. This puts the node of A and B under water. Rest the leaf of A on the rim of the glass, out of the water. 4. Put all three by a bright window, out of strong direct sun.
flow.say: Now we wait. Which one will grow roots first? Write your guess next to each glass.
flow.kid: Put each piece in its own glass. Keep the leaf dry. Put them by a window.

flow.do: On days 4, 7 and 10, count the roots on each cutting. Measure the longest root with the ruler in millimetres. Write the numbers. Pour out the old water and add fresh water.
flow.say: Hold the ruler next to the longest root. Read the millimetres. Is anything happening on C?
flow.kid: Count the roots. Measure the longest one in millimetres. Write it down. Change the water.
flow.parent: Cutting A usually shows small white roots from the node in 7 to 14 days. B may root more slowly, or may sprout a new shoot. C has no node, so they usually grow no roots and may turn soft and brown.

flow.do: On day 14, measure each cutting one last time. Help your child draw a bar chart, one bar for each cutting, showing the longest root in millimetres.
flow.say: Which cutting has the longest roots? Which has none? What does the node do?
flow.kid: Measure one last time. Draw a bar for each cutting. Which one grew most?

check.q: In the Node Test, which money plant cutting is most likely to grow no roots at all?
options: The piece from between two nodes, with no node
The piece with a node and a leaf
The piece with a node but no leaf
check.why: Roots grow from the nodes. A piece with no node has nothing to grow roots from. The leaf helps by making food, so A usually roots fastest.

flow.do: Plant cutting A in a small pot of soil with a drainage hole. Water until a little comes out underneath.
flow.say: You made a new plant from a piece of an old one. Who could you give them to?
flow.kid: Plant your rooted cutting in a pot. Water them gently. Give the plant a name.
flow.parent: If the rooted cutting is not ready, leave them in water a few more days until the roots are about 3 cm long.

experiments.title: Too Much Water? Methi seedlings in three cups
experiments.question: Do methi seedlings grow better with more water, or does a pot need drainage holes too?
experiments.predict: Cup A has holes and gets water only when the soil is dry. Cup B has holes and gets water every day. Cup C has no holes and gets water every day. Which cup will have the most healthy seedlings after 12 days? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three cups are the same size and hold the same amount of the same soil. Each gets 10 methi seeds from the same packet, sown 1 cm deep, and all stand on the same windowsill. Cups B and C get the same 20 ml of water a day. Only the holes and the watering change.

materials.item: 3 plastic cups of the same size (about 200 ml)
a sharp pencil or skewer to poke holes, used by a grown-up
soil from an old pot, or a small bag of potting soil from a nursery
30 methi seeds from the kitchen
a small steel cup or medicine cup to measure 20 ml of water
3 old saucers or plate lids, one under each cup
a ruler with millimetres

experiments.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes. Wash your hands after handling soil.

schedule.what: Poke holes in cups A and B. Fill all three with soil. Sow 10 methi seeds in each. Water all three with 20 ml.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.

Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry. Count the seedlings in each cup: up on day 4, healthy green on day 8. Note any yellow or fallen ones.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.

Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry. Count the seedlings in each cup: up on day 4, healthy green on day 8. Note any yellow or fallen ones.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.
Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry.

Tip out the saucers of A and B. Water B and C with 20 ml. Water A only if the top of the soil feels dry. Count healthy seedlings, measure the tallest, gently tip out each cup and compare the roots. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 4, 8 and 12. On day 12, draw a bar chart of healthy seedlings in each cup, and draw the roots you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out whether giving a plant more water is always better, by growing methi in three cups.

setup.art: A grown-up poking four small holes in the bottom of two plastic cups with a pencil, and a third cup with no holes.
setup.caption: 1. Poke holes in cups A and B only.

setup.art: Three cups filled with soil on a tray, each with 10 methi seeds pressed in.
setup.caption: 2. Fill with soil and sow 10 seeds in each.

setup.art: A child pressing a finger into the soil of cup A, and pouring a small cup of water into cups B and C.
setup.caption: 3. Water B and C daily. Water A only when the soil feels dry.

setup.art: Three cups of methi seedlings on day 12: A and B green and upright, C with yellow, fallen seedlings in dark wet soil.
setup.caption: 4. On day 12, count healthy seedlings and compare.

flow.do: Show your child the three cups. Explain the plan for each. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Cup A has holes and gets water only when the soil is dry. Cup B has holes and gets water every day. Cup C has no holes and gets water every day. Which cup will grow the best methi? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three cups. Which will grow the best methi? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Too Much Water?, a test of whether more water always helps a plant.

flow.do: 1. Poke 4 holes in the bottoms of cups A and B. 2. Fill all three cups with soil to 1 cm below the top. 3. Press 10 methi seeds into each, 1 cm deep. 4. Pour 20 ml of water on each. 5. Stand each cup on its own saucer by a bright window.
flow.say: Every cup gets the same soil, the same seeds and the same window. What is different?
flow.kid: Fill the cups with soil. Press in 10 seeds each. Water each one.

flow.do: Every day, tip out any water in the saucers of cups A and B. Give cups B and C 20 ml of water. Push a finger 1 cm into cup A. Water A only if it feels dry. If water spills over the rim of cup C, skip that day's water for C and write 'full'. Write down which cups you watered.
flow.say: Feel cup A first. Is it dry or damp? Only water when it is dry. Cups B and C get water every day.
flow.kid: Feel cup A with your finger. Dry? Then water. B and C get water every day.

flow.do: On days 4 and 8, count the seedlings in each cup. Write how many are healthy and green, and how many are yellow or have fallen over.
flow.say: Count carefully. Which cup has the most healthy seedlings? Is the soil in cup C different?
flow.kid: Count the green seedlings in each cup. Are any yellow or fallen?
flow.parent: Methi usually comes up in 2 to 4 days. By day 8, cup C often has soggy dark soil with water standing on top, and some seedlings turn yellow or fall over. Cups A and B usually look alike, because the holes let extra water out. If all three look alike, write that down honestly: soil that drains well can hide the harm, and that is a result too.

flow.do: On day 12, count healthy seedlings and measure the tallest in each cup. Then gently tip each cup out onto newspaper and look at the roots.
flow.say: Look at the roots. Are they white and spread out, or brown and short? Which soil smells sour?
flow.kid: Count and measure. Tip out each cup gently. Look at the roots.

check.q: In the Too Much Water? test, cups B and C got the same amount of water. Why did cup C do worse?
options: Cup C had no holes, so water filled the soil and the roots got no air
Cup C got more sunlight
Methi does not like water
check.why: Cups B and C got the same water. Only the holes were different. In cup B, extra water drained away and air came back into the soil. In cup C, the soil stayed soaked, so the roots could not get the oxygen they need.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of healthy seedlings on day 12, one bar for each cup. Then ask for what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each cup. Then say what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer: drainage matters more than the amount of water. Cup C had 3 healthy seedlings and brown roots, while A and B had 9 and 8. Roots need air as well as water.

activities.title: Ask the Elders: our family's plant medicines, and how sure we are

materials.item: a notebook page with a 6-column table
a pencil
a phone, to call a grandparent or an older relative

activities.safety: Write down the remedies, but never make or take one on your own. Some plant remedies are not safe for children.

schedule.what: Interview an elder about plant remedies. Fill in the table. Mark how sure we are about each one.

activities.record: A table with at least 5 plant remedies: plant, part used, used for, who told us, how we know, and how sure we are.
activities.context: In this activity, you collect the plant remedies your family knows, and then ask a scientist's question about each one: how do we know it works?

setup.art: A girl holding a phone on speaker, writing in a notebook while her grandmother talks on the other end.
setup.caption: 1. Ask an elder which plants they use for health.

setup.art: A notebook table with columns: Plant, Part, Used for, Who told us, How we know, How sure.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in the table for each remedy.

setup.art: Three coloured stickers on the table: green for tested and works, yellow for not tested, red for tested and did not work.
setup.caption: 3. Mark how sure we are about each one.

flow.do: Draw the table with six columns: Plant, Part used, Used for, Who told us, How we know, How sure are we.
flow.say: Our elders know many plant remedies. Let's collect them, like a scientist collects samples. Then we'll ask how we know each one works.
flow.kid: Draw a table with six columns. You are going to interview an elder.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ask the Elders. You collect your family's plant remedies.

flow.do: Call or sit with a grandparent, an older aunt or a neighbour. Your child asks the questions and writes the answers. Aim for at least five remedies.
flow.say: Ask them: which plants do you use when someone is unwell? Which part of the plant? Who taught you? How do you know it helps?
flow.kid: Ask your elder: which plants help when we are ill? Which part? Who taught you?
flow.parent: Common answers include tulsi leaves in kadha, ajwain seeds for a stomach ache, ginger for a cough, haldi in milk, neem leaves in bath water, and curry leaves or methi in food.

flow.do: For each remedy, fill in 'How sure are we?' together. Green: tested in a fair trial in people and found to work. Yellow: not tested fairly yet, or not settled. Red: tested fairly and did not work. Look up one or two with your child.
flow.say: Our elders saw these help. But many illnesses get better on their own. So which of these have been tested fairly? Let's find out for one.
flow.kid: Mark each remedy green, yellow or red. Green means tested and it works.
flow.parent: Most home remedies will be yellow. That is honest, not an insult to the elder. Ginger for feeling sick has some good trials. Haldi milk for a cold has not been settled by a large fair trial.

flow.do: Count how many of each colour you have. Talk about it together.
flow.say: How many are green? How many are yellow? How could a scientist turn a yellow one into green or red?
flow.kid: Count your greens, yellows and reds. How could we test a yellow one?

check.q: A girl's grandmother says tulsi kadha cured her cold in five days. Why is this not enough to show that tulsi kadha works?
options: A cold often gets better in about a week anyway, so we need a fair comparison with a control group
Grandmothers always remember wrongly
Tulsi is poisonous
check.why: The grandmother really did get better. But colds usually get better on their own in about a week. Only a fair trial, with some people who drink kadha and some who drink a similar drink without tulsi, can show whether the tulsi helped.

activities.title: Indian or Visitor? Where did the trees near us come from?

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
the list of trees and where they came from, in this activity's first step
a grown-up's phone to look up any tree not on the list, if you like

activities.safety: Look from a window or balcony, or walk with a grown-up and stay off the road.

schedule.what: Spot trees and plants near your home. Look up where each first came from. Count Indian and visitor plants.

activities.record: A list of the plants you saw, each marked 'Indian' or 'Visitor from' with the place, and a tally of each.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out which of the trees and plants near your home are native to India and which were brought from far away.

setup.art: A child on a balcony pointing at a street with a neem, a gulmohar, a coconut palm and a eucalyptus.
setup.caption: 1. Spot trees and plants from your window or street.

setup.art: A list in a notebook with each tree name and a small flag drawing for where they came from.
setup.caption: 2. Write where each one first came from.

setup.art: Two tally columns, Indian and Visitor, with marks in each.
setup.caption: 3. Count Indian and visitor plants.

flow.do: Read the list together. Native to India: neem, peepal, banyan, mango, jamun, amaltas, palash, arjun, ashoka, black pepper and tulsi. Visitors: tamarind (Africa), gulmohar (Madagascar), eucalyptus (Australia), rain tree and subabul (Central and South America). More visitors: papaya and chilli (the Americas), bougainvillea (South America) and money plant (islands in the Pacific).
flow.say: Some plants grew in India before any people brought plants from far away. Others came on ships, with traders, rulers and gardeners. Which do you think are the most common near us?
flow.kid: Read the list. Some plants are Indian. Some came from far away. Guess which kind is most common here.
flow.context: This is the first step of Indian or Visitor?, a hunt for native and visiting plants near your home.
flow.parent: Coconut is hard to place. Coconuts float, and people carried them too, so scientists still argue where coconuts first grew. Count coconut as 'still argued'.

flow.do: From your windows, balcony or a short walk, find as many different trees and big plants as you can. Write each one down. Mark it Indian or Visitor using the list. Look up any you don't know.
flow.say: What is that tree? Is it on our list? Indian or visitor?
flow.kid: Find trees and plants. Write each name. Mark it Indian or Visitor.

flow.do: Make a tally of Indian and visitor plants. Work out which is more.
flow.say: Did you guess right? Why might so many visitors grow along roads and in parks?
flow.kid: Count Indian and Visitor plants. Which has more?

check.q: Tamarind is used in rasam all over South India. Where did the tamarind tree first grow?
options: Africa
Kerala
Australia
check.why: Tamarind first grew in Africa and reached India long ago. Now it is so common that many people think it is Indian. Its scientific name, Tamarindus indica, even says 'of India'.

activities.title: A Passport for an Indian Plant

materials.item: an outline map of India: trace one from an atlas or the school book, or draw it by hand
a sheet of paper folded in half like a passport
crayons or colour pencils

schedule.what: Choose an endemic Indian plant. Mark where they grow on a map. Make their passport.

activities.record: A plant passport with a drawing, names, home on the map, what makes the plant special, dangers and who protects them.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a passport for a plant who grows naturally only in India, or only in India and Sri Lanka.

setup.art: Four small picture cards: neelakurinji, red sanders, a pitcher plant and a talipot palm.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one plant.

setup.art: An outline map of India with one coloured patch where the chosen plant grows.
setup.caption: 2. Colour where they grow on the map.

setup.art: A folded paper passport with a drawing of the plant on the cover and boxes of writing inside.
setup.caption: 3. Fill in the plant's passport.

flow.do: Read the four plant cards aloud. Neelakurinji: a shrub on the high hills of the Nilgiris, Munnar and Kodaikanal, who blooms blue once in 12 years. Red sanders: a tree with deep red wood, wild only in the southern Eastern Ghats near Tirupati, endangered by smuggling. Nepenthes khasiana: a pitcher plant who catches insects, wild only in Meghalaya. Talipot palm: grows on the west coast and in Sri Lanka, flowers once after 30 to 80 years, then dies.
flow.say: Each of these plants grows wild in only one part of the world. Which one would you like to make a passport for?
flow.kid: Listen to the four plants. Choose one for your passport.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Passport for an Indian Plant.

flow.do: Help your child colour the plant's home on the map of India. Mark the state names.
flow.say: Where does your plant live? Why might a plant live only on high hills, or only in one hill range?
flow.kid: Colour where your plant lives on the map. Write the state.

flow.do: Your child fills in the passport. Name in English and one Indian language. Scientific name. Home. What makes them special. Dangers they face. Who protects them. Then draw them on the cover.
flow.say: A passport tells who someone is and where they belong. What does your plant need to stay alive in their home?
flow.kid: Fill in your plant's passport. Draw your plant on the cover.
flow.parent: Scientific names: neelakurinji is Strobilanthes kunthiana, red sanders is Pterocarpus santalinus, the pitcher plant is Nepenthes khasiana, the talipot palm is Corypha umbraculifera.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let's check one idea.
flow.kid: Answer the question.

check.q: A plant is endemic to Meghalaya. What does that mean?
options: They grow wild only in Meghalaya and nowhere else on Earth
They grow everywhere in India
They were brought to Meghalaya from another country
check.why: Endemic means found naturally in one place only. Nepenthes khasiana is endemic to Meghalaya. If their wild home is lost, the wild plants are lost for good.

activities.title: Finger Test: when does a pot plant really need water?

materials.item: a pot plant at home with a drainage hole, like a tulsi, money plant or curry leaf
a kitchen scale, if you have one
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Water the pot until water comes out of the hole. Weigh or lift it. Feel the soil.
Feel the soil 2 cm down. Weigh or lift the pot. Water only if it is dry.
Feel, weigh and decide again.
Feel, weigh and decide again.
Feel, weigh and decide again.
Feel, weigh and decide again.
Feel and weigh. Look at the week. How many days did the plant need water?

activities.record: A 7-day table: day, soil feels wet, damp or dry, pot weight or heavy or light, watered or not.
activities.context: In this activity, you learn to tell when a pot plant needs water, by feeling the soil and weighing the pot every day for a week.

setup.art: A child pushing one finger into the soil of a tulsi pot, up to the first line of the finger.
setup.caption: 1. Push a finger 2 cm into the soil.

setup.art: A pot standing on a kitchen scale showing a number in grams.
setup.caption: 2. Weigh the pot, or lift it and feel how heavy it is.

setup.art: A table with seven rows and ticks for days the plant was watered.
setup.caption: 3. Water only when the soil is dry. Write it down.

flow.do: On day 1, water the pot slowly until a little water comes out of the hole. Then weigh the pot, or let your child lift it and feel how heavy it is.
flow.say: This is how heavy the pot is when the soil is full of water. Every day we will check how much lighter it gets.
flow.kid: Water your pot until a little comes out underneath. Weigh it, or lift it.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Finger Test, a week of learning when a pot plant needs water.

flow.do: Each day, your child pushes a finger 2 cm into the soil and says wet, damp or dry. Then weigh or lift the pot. Water only if the soil is dry 2 cm down.
flow.say: How does the soil feel today? Is the pot lighter than yesterday? Does our plant need water today?
flow.kid: Feel the soil. Wet, damp or dry? Weigh the pot. Only water if it is dry.
flow.parent: Water leaves the pot through the leaves and from the soil surface. A pot often gets lighter by tens of grams a day in summer. In the monsoon, it may stay damp for days.

flow.do: On day 7, look at the table together. Count how many days the plant needed water.
flow.say: Our plant needed water on only some days. What would have happened if we watered every day?
flow.kid: How many days did your plant need water? Was it every day?

check.q: A pot feels damp 2 cm down, and the pot still feels heavy. What should you do?
options: Wait, and check again tomorrow
Water a lot, to be safe
Move the plant into a dark cupboard
check.why: Damp soil still has water for the roots. Adding more would fill the air gaps and could rot the roots. Checking first is how good gardeners care for a plant.

activities.title: Press a Medicine Plant: make a botanist's sheet

materials.item: a small sprig of tulsi, curry leaf or mint from your kitchen or a pot
old newspaper
a few heavy books
a sheet of thick paper and some tape

schedule.what: Lay the sprig flat in newspaper. Press under heavy books.
Take out the dry sprig. Tape it to the sheet. Write the label like a botanist.

activities.record: A herbarium sheet: a pressed sprig with a label giving the names, the date, the place, the collector, the part used and how sure we are about the use.
activities.context: In this activity, you press a medicine plant and label them the way botanists do, so the sheet can be kept for years.

setup.art: A sprig of tulsi laid flat inside a folded newspaper, with leaves spread out.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the sprig flat in newspaper.

setup.art: A pile of heavy books on top of the newspaper.
setup.caption: 2. Press under heavy books for a week.

setup.art: A thick sheet with the dried sprig taped down and a neat label in the bottom corner.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the sprig to a sheet and write the label.

flow.do: Choose a sprig with a few leaves. Lay it flat inside folded newspaper, spreading the leaves so they do not overlap. Put several heavy books on top. Leave for a week in a dry place.
flow.say: Botanists have pressed plants like this for hundreds of years. A pressed sheet can last for more than a century. Why might that be useful?
flow.kid: Lay your sprig flat in newspaper. Spread the leaves. Put heavy books on top.
flow.context: This is the first step of Press a Medicine Plant. You make a botanist's sheet.
flow.wait: Leave under the books for 7 days
flow.parent: In humid weather, change the newspaper after 2 days so the sprig does not go mouldy. The sprig is ready when it feels stiff and papery. If it is still soft after a week, press it a few days more.

flow.do: After a week, take out the dry sprig. Tape it gently to the thick paper. Write the label in the bottom right corner. Give the names in English and two Indian languages, and the scientific name. Then add the date, place, collector, part used, use and how sure we are.
flow.say: Every label says who collected the plant, where and when. Then anyone in the future can trust the sheet.
flow.kid: Tape your sprig to the paper. Write the label in the corner.
flow.parent: Scientific names: tulsi is Ocimum tenuiflorum, curry leaf is Murraya koenigii, mint is Mentha. The botanist E. K. Janaki Ammal, from Thalassery in Kerala, spent her last years studying medicine plants near Chennai.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let's check one idea.
flow.kid: Answer the question.

check.q: Why does a botanist write the date and the place on every pressed plant?
options: So that anyone later can know where and when the plant grew, and compare
To make the sheet look nice
Because pressed plants need a birthday
check.why: A sheet with a date and a place is a piece of evidence. Scientists can compare old sheets with plants today to see which plants have disappeared from a place.

projects.title: A Kitchen Herb Pot: grow mint and lemongrass from market stems

materials.item: a bunch of fresh mint from the vegetable shop
2 or 3 lemongrass stalks with the white bottom end still on, if your market sells them. Skip them if not
2 glasses of water
a pot at least 15 cm wide with a drainage hole, and soil
a ruler with millimetres
a notebook for the herb diary

projects.safety: Wash your hands after handling soil.

schedule.what: Strip the lower leaves from 5 mint stems. Stand them in water. Stand the lemongrass in water too.
Count roots on each stem. Measure the longest. Change the water.
Plant the rooted stems in the pot. Water until it drains.
Finger test. Measure the tallest mint shoot. Count new leaves.
Finger test. Measure again. Count new leaves.
Finger test and measure again. Draw a line graph of the tallest shoot. Pick a few leaves for chutney.

projects.record: A herb diary with root counts, shoot heights on days 14, 21 and 28, a line graph, and a note on each watering.
projects.context: In this 4-week project, you grow a pot of mint, and lemongrass if you can, from stems bought at the market.

setup.art: Five mint stems with their lower leaves removed, standing in a glass of water, with small white roots at the nodes.
setup.caption: 1. Stand mint stems in water. Roots grow from the nodes.

setup.art: A child planting rooted mint stems into a pot of soil with a hole at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Plant the rooted stems in a pot.

setup.art: A ruler held up against the tallest mint shoot in the pot.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the tallest shoot each week.

flow.do: 1. Pick 5 healthy mint stems. 2. Strip the leaves from the bottom 5 cm of each. 3. Stand them in a glass of water with the bare part under water. 4. Do the same with lemongrass if you have it.
flow.say: We took the bottom leaves off so the nodes are under water. Where do you think the roots will grow?
flow.kid: Take the bottom leaves off five mint stems. Stand them in water.
flow.context: This is the first day of A Kitchen Herb Pot, a 4-week project growing herbs from market stems.

flow.do: On day 7, count the roots on each stem and measure the longest. Change the water.
flow.say: Look where the roots are coming from. Are they at the nodes?
flow.kid: Count the roots. Measure the longest one. Are they at the nodes?
flow.parent: Mint usually grows white roots at the nodes within a week. Lemongrass is slower, often 2 to 3 weeks.

flow.do: On day 10, plant the rooted mint stems in the pot, about 5 cm deep. Water slowly until a little comes out of the hole. Put the pot where they get a few hours of sun. Keep any lemongrass in water until its roots are about 2 cm long, then plant the lemongrass too.
flow.say: Now we care for them. Remember the finger test. When do we water?
flow.kid: Plant your rooted stems. Water until a little comes out underneath.

flow.do: On days 14, 21 and 28, do the finger test, measure the tallest shoot and count new leaves. Write it in the diary.
flow.say: How much taller is the mint this week? Did the soil need water today?
flow.kid: Measure your tallest mint. Count new leaves. Feel the soil.

flow.do: On day 28, draw a line graph of the tallest shoot on days 14, 21 and 28. Then pick a few leaves together for chutney or tea.
flow.say: You grew this from a market bunch. What did the plant need from you? What did you get from the plant?
flow.kid: Draw a line graph. Then pick a few leaves to eat.

check.q: Why did the mint grow roots when the lower leaves were stripped off and the stems stood in water?
options: The nodes under the water can grow roots
Water makes any stem grow roots
Mint leaves grow roots
check.why: Roots grow from the nodes. Stripping the lower leaves put the nodes under water. A bare piece of stem with no node would not root.

challenges.title: Holiday Water: keep a pot plant alive for a week alone
challenges.problem: Your family is going away for 7 days, and nobody can come in to water the plants. Design a way to keep one pot plant watered for the whole week, without drowning the roots.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Nobody may touch the plant for 7 days.
The roots must not sit in standing water.
Measure how much water your design uses.
materials: a pot plant with a drainage hole
a plastic bottle or a small steel bucket
a strip of old cotton vest, cotton string or a shoelace
a nail or skewer (used by a grown-up)
a small clay pot or kulhad
general: A wick: put one end of a cotton strip in a bowl of water and push the other end into the soil. Water climbs up the cotton into the soil.
A drip bottle: a grown-up makes a tiny hole in a bottle cap. Fill the bottle and push it upside down into the soil.
Move the pot out of direct sun and cover the soil with dry leaves, so less water escapes.
creative: Bury a small unglazed clay pot, like a kulhad, in a big pot of soil and fill it with water. Water seeps slowly through the clay into the soil. Farmers in many dry places have used buried clay pots like this for centuries.
Make a clear plastic bag tent over the plant, held up with sticks, so water that leaves the leaves drips back.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design and test it for 3 days before the real trip. Measure how much water it used each day. Was the soil damp but not soaked?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about caring for plants. You keep a pot plant watered for a week while nobody is home.

setup.art: A pot plant next to a bowl of water, with a cotton strip running from the bowl into the soil.
setup.caption: 1. Try a wick from a bowl of water.

setup.art: An upside-down plastic bottle pushed into a pot of soil, with a few drops coming out of the cap.
setup.caption: 2. Or try a slow drip bottle.

setup.art: A child measuring how much water is left in the bowl with a measuring cup.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how much water your design used.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the pot plant you will use.
flow.say: We need to give this plant water for 7 days, but not too much. What happens if the soil stays soaked?
flow.kid: Your plant must get water for 7 days alone. What could go wrong?
flow.context: This is the first step of Holiday Water, a design challenge for caring for a plant while you are away.

flow.do: Your child draws two or three ideas, then chooses one to build.
flow.say: Which idea gives water slowly? Which is easiest to build?
flow.kid: Draw two or three ideas. Choose one to build.

flow.do: Build the design. Measure the water you start with. Leave it for 3 days. Do the finger test each day and measure the water left.
flow.say: How much water did the design use each day? Is the soil damp, or soaked, or dry?
flow.kid: Build it. Measure the water. Check the soil every day for 3 days.

flow.do: Look at the results. Improve the design if the soil was too wet or too dry.
flow.say: What would you change before the real trip?
flow.kid: Was the soil too wet or too dry? What will you change?

check.q: A wick of cotton string carries water from a bowl up into a pot. Why does the water move up the string?
options: Water creeps along the tiny gaps between the cotton threads
The plant sucks the bowl dry with a pump
Cotton makes new water
check.why: Water is drawn into narrow gaps, like those between cotton threads, and creeps along them. As the soil dries, more water moves up the string.

challenges.title: Design a Fair Trial: does tulsi kadha help a cold get better faster?
challenges.problem: Many families give tulsi kadha for a cold. Design a fair trial that could really find out whether it helps people get better faster. You plan it on paper only. You do not test it on anyone.
constraints: This is a plan on paper. Do not give anyone kadha or anything else as part of this challenge.
Nobody may be given anything unsafe.
Nobody who needs a doctor's medicine may be kept from it.
The trial must be fair: only one thing can differ between the groups.
materials: the explanation card 'How scientists test an old remedy'
general: Two groups of people with colds, the same size and similar ages.
One group drinks tulsi kadha. The control group drinks a drink that looks and tastes much the same, with no tulsi.
Count how many days each person takes to feel better.
Nobody knows which drink they had until the end.
creative: Ask the people's doctors to judge when each person is better, without telling the doctors who drank which drink.
Use many families across India, in Chennai, Kolkata, Pune and Guwahati, so the result is not just about one city's weather.
challenges.your_turn: Write your plan: how many people, what each group drinks, what you measure, how you keep it fair and how you keep everyone safe. Then say what result would show that kadha helps.
challenges.context: This is a thinking challenge. You design, on paper, a fair trial of a home remedy.

setup.art: Two groups of stick figures on paper, labelled kadha and control, each with 20 people.
setup.caption: 1. Plan two groups of the same size.

setup.art: Two identical steel cups, one secretly marked with a dot underneath.
setup.caption: 2. Make the drinks look the same, so nobody knows which they have.

setup.art: A table with two columns of numbers: days to get better in each group.
setup.caption: 3. Plan what you will measure.

flow.do: Read the problem together.
flow.say: If someone drinks kadha and gets better in five days, does that prove the kadha worked? Why not?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Does getting better prove the kadha worked?
flow.context: This is the first step of Design a Fair Trial, a thinking challenge about testing a remedy.

flow.do: Your child plans the trial on paper: who takes part, what each group gets, and what is measured.
flow.say: What would the control group drink? How would you stop people guessing which group they are in?
flow.kid: Plan two groups. What does each group drink? What do you measure?

flow.do: Ask your child how they would keep the trial safe and fair. Write the answers.
flow.say: What if someone gets very ill during the trial? What must happen?
flow.kid: How do you keep everyone safe? How do you keep it fair?
flow.parent: Good answers: anyone who gets worse sees a doctor at once and takes any medicine they need. Real trials are checked by a group of doctors and other people before they begin.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Let's check one idea.
flow.kid: Answer the question.

check.q: In a fair trial of kadha, why should the control group get a drink that looks and tastes like kadha?
options: So people cannot tell which group they are in, because believing you got a remedy can make you feel better
Because kadha is too expensive
So the control group also gets the tulsi
check.why: Feeling cared for can make people feel better. If both groups get a similar drink, any extra difference can only come from the tulsi.

items.p: Why do many plants make bitter, smelly or hot chemicals?
opts: To protect themselves from insects, animals and moulds
To make food taste nice for people
Because they are old and going bad
items.why: A plant cannot run away, so many plants protect themselves with chemistry. People found these chemicals useful later. Picking 'to make food taste nice' is a common idea, but the chemicals were there long before anyone cooked.

items.p: A clove is which part of the clove tree?
items.why: Cloves are flower buds picked before they open and dried in the sun. Look at the little ball on top: that is the unopened flower.

items.p: In Spice Guard, the four potato squares are left open for 30 minutes so that mould spores from the air can land on every square.
items.why: True. Spores float in the air everywhere. Leaving every square open for the same time gives each one the same chance to catch spores, so the test stays fair.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: In a test, the part where you add nothing new, so you can compare, is called the ____.
items.why: The plain potato square in Spice Guard is the control. It shows what happens anyway.

items.p: Match each plant to how they protect themselves.
pairs: a bitter chemical that stops insects eating
a chemical that burns mammals' mouths
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Plants protect themselves in many ways: with chemicals, thorns, sticky sap and more.

items.p: Revathi, a girl in Class 4 in Kochi, did Spice Guard. On day 6 she counted these mouldy squares out of 16: plain 12, rice flour 13, haldi 5, clove 0. How many more mouldy squares did the plain potato have than the haldi potato?
items.why: 12 take away 5 is 7. Haldi slowed the mould a lot, but did not stop them completely.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: Revathi tested only one potato square of each kind. Why would her result be more trustworthy if she repeated the test with three squares of each kind and compared the averages?
items.a: One square could be different by chance, for example it might catch more spores or be a little wetter. If three squares of the same kind give similar numbers, we can trust the result more. If they differ a lot, we know one square is not enough.
items.why: A strong answer says that one result can be luck, and that repeating the test shows whether the result is steady.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: Sort these plants: native to India, or a visitor from another land?
items.a: as given
items.why: Neem, peepal, amaltas and black pepper grew in India before people brought plants from far away. Gulmohar came from Madagascar, chilli and papaya from the Americas, and eucalyptus from Australia.
items.context: In Indian or Visitor?, you looked at plants near your home and found out where each first came from.

items.p: A plant remedy is natural, so the remedy is always safe for children.
items.why: False. Plant defence chemicals are strong on purpose. Clove oil and neem oil have badly poisoned small children who swallowed them. The dose decides.

items.p: Why does a pot need a hole at the bottom?
opts: So extra water can drain out and air can get back to the roots
items.why: Roots need water and air. Without a hole, water fills every gap in the soil and the roots can rot.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Neelakurinji, red sanders, Nepenthes khasiana, gulmohar.
items.a: Gulmohar, because gulmohar came from Madagascar. The other three are endemic to India: they grow wild only in India.
items.why: Endemic plants grow wild in only one place. Gulmohar grows in many countries, and came to India from Madagascar.

items.p: Draw a money plant stem with two leaves. Label a node. Draw where new roots would grow on a cutting.
items.a: A stem with two leaves, a node labelled where each leaf joins, and roots drawn coming from the node.
items.why: Roots grow from the nodes. A strong drawing shows the roots at the node, not in the middle of the bare stem.
items.context: In the Node Test, you stood three money plant cuttings in water: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node and no leaf, and one with no node.

items.p: Kavin, a boy of six, watered his tulsi three times a day because he loved them. The leaves turned yellow and drooped. Explain to Kavin what went wrong, in words he will understand.
items.a: Roots need air as well as water. When you water too much, the soil stays full of water and there is no air left for the roots. Then the roots start to rot, and the leaves droop. Feel the soil first, and only water when it is dry.
items.why: A strong answer says roots need air, links soaked soil to rotting roots, and gives Kavin a clear thing to do: check the soil first.

items.p: A company makes a new tonic from a forest fruit. A forest community showed scientists the fruit, and had eaten it for generations.

views.who: Selvi, from the forest community (an imagined view)
views.says: My grandparents found this fruit and kept the forest safe. If you earn money from it, our village should share it.

views.who: A scientist at the company (an imagined view)
views.says: We spent ten years testing the fruit to make sure the tonic is safe. That cost a lot of money. We need to earn it back.

items.ask: Who do you think should get money from the tonic, and how much? Give a reason. Then say one fair point the other person made.
items.a: Any answer with a reason and a fair point from the other side. For example: the community should get a share, because they found the fruit and kept it safe. But the scientist is right that testing costs money, so the company should also earn something. That is what happened with the Kani people of Kerala and the tonic Jeevani.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and fairly states the other side's point. It may mention the Kani and Jeevani as a real example.

items.p: Neelakurinji covered the hills of Munnar in blue in 2018. About how often does a neelakurinji plant bloom?
items.why: Neelakurinji grows for about 12 years, then all the plants on a hillside bloom together, make seeds and die. Nobody yet knows how they keep count.

items.p: A tomato leaf is chewed by a caterpillar. What happens to the plant's other leaves?
opts: Signals travel to them and they make more defence chemicals
Nothing, only the bitten leaf changes
items.why: Plants sense a bite and send signals around their body. Other leaves get ready before the caterpillar reaches them. Picking 'only the bitten leaf' is a common idea, but scientists have measured the signals.

items.p: Birds eat red chillies without any trouble, but mice avoid them. How does this help the chilli plant?
items.a: A mouse chews the seeds and crushes them, so they never grow. A bird swallows the seeds whole and drops them somewhere new, where they can sprout. Capsaicin keeps the seed-crushers away but lets the seed-carriers eat.
items.why: A strong answer explains what each animal does to the seeds, and links the burn to who it keeps away.

items.p: Put these steps of the Spice Guard test in the right order.
a: Leave them open to the air for 30 minutes
Add a powder to three squares and leave one plain
Close the boxes and keep them in a cupboard
Count the mouldy squares each day
items.why: The squares must catch spores before they are covered and closed. Then you count each day, and draw the graph at the end.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: Mitali, a girl in Kolkata, put three money plant cuttings in water. After 14 days, cutting A had 5 roots, cutting B had 2 roots, and cutting C had none. Which cutting had no node?
items.why: Roots grow from the nodes. A cutting with no node grows no roots.
items.context: In the Node Test, you stood three money plant cuttings in water: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node and no leaf, and one with no node.

items.p: In the Node Test, cutting A, with a node and a leaf, rooted faster than cutting B, with a node and no leaf. Why might the leaf help?
items.a: The leaf makes food from sunlight. The cutting can use that food to build new roots. Without a leaf, cutting B has only the food stored in their stem.
items.why: A strong answer links the leaf to making food, and food to building roots.
items.context: In the Node Test, you stood three money plant cuttings in water: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node and no leaf, and one with no node.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: studied chemicals in Indian plants and helped make Ayush-56
tested sarpagandha on patients with high blood pressure
studied sacred groves in the Western Ghats
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of them helped India's plant knowledge be tested, protected or credited.

items.p: A cold that gets better after a week of haldi milk proves that haldi milk cures colds.
items.why: False. Colds usually get better in about a week anyway. Only a fair trial with a control group could show whether haldi milk helped.

items.p: Gardeners say more pot plants die from too much water than too little. What is the best way to know when to water?
opts: Push a finger 2 cm into the soil, and water only if it feels dry
Water at the same time every day, whatever the weather
Wait until the leaves turn brown
items.why: The finger test tells you what the soil needs today. In the monsoon a pot may stay damp for days, while in May it may dry out every day.

items.p: A city council in Tamil Nadu is deciding whether to remove seemai karuvelam, also called vilayati babul, from the land around a lake. This tree came from Mexico and Central America and now grows everywhere.

views.says: Seemai karuvelam takes a lot of water from the ground and crowds out native plants. We should remove them and plant native trees.

views.who: Gopal, who collects firewood (an imagined view)
views.says: These trees give my family firewood every day, and they grow where nothing else will. Remove them, and we have nothing.
I build my nest in these thorny branches, safe from snakes.

items.ask: What should the council do? Give your reason. Then answer back from one of the other views.
items.a: Any reasoned answer. For example: remove them slowly and plant native trees like neem and vagai at the same time, so families still get firewood and birds still have nesting trees. A strong answer weighs water, native plants, people and birds.
items.why: Real choices about invasive plants have costs and benefits for people, for native plants and for other animals. A strong answer weighs more than one side.

items.p: Draw the line graph from these Spice Guard results. Plain potato: day 2 is 0, day 3 is 2, day 4 is 5, day 5 is 9, day 6 is 12. Clove potato: 0 every day.
items.a: Days 2 to 6 along the bottom, mouldy squares 0 to 16 up the side. One line climbing from 0 to 12, and one flat line at 0.
items.why: A line graph shows how something changes over time. The steep line shows mould spreading fast. The flat line shows the clove kept the mould away.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: Sakshi says, 'Our tulsi kadha must work, because my great-grandmother used it.' Is she right? What would you need to find out?
items.a: Not yet. The kadha might work, but being old only shows that people trusted the kadha. We need a fair trial: two groups of people with colds, one drinking kadha and one drinking a similar drink without tulsi, and compare how fast they get better.
items.why: A strong answer respects the tradition but says age is not proof, and describes a fair comparison.

items.p: Why are there so many endemic plants in the Western Ghats and the hills of Meghalaya?
opts: Their plants were cut off from other places for a very long time, so new kinds grew there
Endemic plants only grow in rain
items.why: Hills and islands keep plants apart from other places. Over a long time, new kinds of plants grow there and nowhere else.

items.p: A plant brought from another land who spreads so fast that they crowd out native plants is called an ____ plant.
items.why: Lantana and water hyacinth are invasive plants in India.

items.p: Every plant that was brought to India from another land harms the native plants.
items.why: False. Most visitors, like papaya and chilli, live quietly beside native plants. Only a few, like lantana and water hyacinth, spread so fast that they crowd out others.

items.p: A drop of clove oil can ease a toothache, but a child who drinks clove oil can become very ill. How can the same chemical help and harm?
items.a: The chemical is strong, because the clove made it to protect themselves. A tiny amount on one tooth numbs it a little. A large amount swallowed reaches the whole body and harms it. The dose decides.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of dose and explains why defence chemicals are strong.

items.p: Arun says, 'Spice Guard proves that clove powder will cure an infection on my skin.' Explain what Spice Guard does show and what it does not.
items.a: Spice Guard shows that clove powder stopped mould growing on potato in a box. It does not show that clove is safe on skin, that it works inside a person's body, or that it cures an infection. Those need tests in people, done by doctors, with the right dose.
items.why: A strong answer separates a laboratory result on food from a cure in people, and mentions safety and dose.
items.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

items.p: In 1995, a patent office in America gave two researchers a patent for using turmeric powder to heal wounds. Indian scientists showed old Indian texts that described this use, and the patent was cancelled in 1997.

views.who: R. A. Mashelkar, the scientist who led India's challenge
views.says: Indian families have used turmeric on wounds for centuries. You cannot patent what is already known. That would be taking our knowledge.
The old Indian texts were not in our library and not in English. We could not check them before we gave the patent.

items.ask: Who was right? What should patent offices and India each do so this does not happen again?
items.a: A strong answer says the patent was wrong because the use was already known, but understands that the officer could not read the texts. Good solutions: India puts old knowledge into a library patent officers can search, which India did with the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library. Patent offices check such libraries before they give a patent.
items.why: Both sides have a point. A strong answer finds a solution that respects both, like the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library.

items.p: Suppose that in Too Much Water?, cup A, with holes and watered only when dry, got about half as much water as cup B over 12 days. Both cups grew about the same number of healthy seedlings. What would this show?
opts: Watering every day was not needed, because the soil in cup A still had enough water
Methi grows better with no water at all
Cup B had too little water
items.why: Cup A got water only when the soil was dry, and did just as well. Extra water drained out of cup B and was wasted. The plant needed some water, not as much as possible.
items.context: In Too Much Water?, you grew methi in three cups: A with holes, watered when dry, B with holes, watered daily, and C with no holes, watered daily.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether dry neem leaves keep weevils out of rice. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would measure.
items.a: Use two tins of the same size, filled with the same amount of the same rice. Put 10 dry neem leaves in one and nothing in the other. Keep both in the same cupboard for the same time. After a month, count the weevils in a cup of rice from each tin.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the neem leaves, keeps the rice, tins, place and time the same, and measures something countable.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Eugenol, azadirachtin, capsaicin, latex.
items.a: Latex, because latex is a sticky sap that works by gluing insects' mouths. The other three are chemicals that work by being smelly, bitter or burning.
items.why: Eugenol (clove and tulsi), azadirachtin (neem) and capsaicin (chilli) are defence chemicals that act on the attacker's body. Latex works mostly by being sticky. Other answers can be right if well argued.

items.p: Sarpagandha root has been used in India for centuries. Doctors in Europe ignored it until 1949. What changed their minds?
opts: A careful study of patients by Rustom Jal Vakil, published in a heart journal
A famous person said it worked
items.why: Vakil's careful study of patients was evidence that doctors everywhere could check. Indian doctors had already reported it in 1931, but few people abroad paid attention.

items.p: Neelakurinji plants on a hillside all bloom in the same year, about every 12 years. Suggest one reason why it might help them to bloom all together, instead of a few each year.
items.a: If they all bloom together, they make far more seeds than seed-eaters can eat, so some seeds are left to grow. Bees and other insects also have many flowers to visit at once. Scientists are not sure which reason is right.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason linked to seeds or pollinators, and notes that this is still not certain.

items.p: Design a sign for the gate of a sacred grove that tells visitors why the grove matters and what they must not do. Draw and write it.
items.a: A sign with a picture of the grove and two or three reasons, such as old trees, rare plants, a spring, and rules like 'Do not cut or pick anything'.
items.why: A strong sign gives both the community's reasons and the scientists' reasons, like rare plants and water.

items.p: Most medicine plants sold in India are still collected from the wild, not grown on farms.
items.why: True. That is why some, like sarpagandha, have become scarce in the wild. Growing them on farms helps protect the wild plants.

items.p: In a fair trial of a cold remedy, 20 people drink the remedy and 20 drink a placebo. In the remedy group, 14 are better in 5 days. In the placebo group, 13 are better in 5 days. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The remedy made almost no difference, because both groups got better at about the same rate
The remedy works, because 14 people got better
items.why: 14 and 13 are very close. With only 20 people in each group, a difference of one person could be luck. The remedy did not show a clear effect in this trial.

items.p: Paati, the grandmother in the story The Leaves Nobody Ate, says the neem senses a caterpillar's bite and looks after themselves. A plant scientist says the response is automatic, built by evolution. Write what each one would point to as evidence. Which view do you lean towards, and why?
items.a: Paati would point to how the plant senses the bite and changes their other leaves, as if they knew what was happening. The scientist would point to how plants that happened to make these chemicals survived better over millions of years, so the response is built in. Any reasoned choice is fine.
items.why: A strong answer states both views fairly with evidence, and gives a reason for the child's own choice.

items.p: Match each plant who flowers rarely to how often they bloom.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These plants wait many years, flower all at once, make seeds and die. How they keep count is not known.

items.p: Sort these ways to care for a pot plant into 'good care' and 'harmful'.
items: checking the soil with a finger before watering
a pot with a drainage hole
watering until a little comes out underneath
a saucer always full of water under the pot
watering three times a day in the monsoon
items.a: as given
items.why: Roots need water and air. Good care gives water when the soil is dry and lets extra water drain away.

items.p: Asima Chatterjee was the first woman to earn a Doctor of Science degree from an Indian university, in 1944. Why do you think it took so long for a woman to earn one? What might have been lost?
items.a: Many families and universities did not let girls study science, and few women were given labs or jobs. Many women who could have found medicines never had the chance. So discoveries were lost or delayed.
items.why: A strong answer names real barriers, like who was allowed to study, and says what science loses when people are left out.

items.p: A plant has a chemical that kills mould on food in a box. What should scientists test next, before anyone uses the chemical as a medicine?
opts: Whether the chemical is safe for people, and what dose is needed
Whether the plant has nice flowers
items.why: A laboratory test is only the first step. Next come careful tests of safety and dose, then fair trials in people.

quiz.p: Neem leaves taste bitter. Who is the bitterness mainly for?
opts: The neem, to keep insects from eating the leaves
quiz.why: The neem was bitter long before people used neem leaves. People borrowed the neem's protection later.

quiz.p: Which chemical makes a chilli hot?
quiz.why: Capsaicin burns the mouths of mammals. Curcumin is the yellow in haldi, and eugenol is the smell of clove.

quiz.p: In Spice Guard, which square is the control?
opts: The plain potato with nothing added
quiz.why: The control has nothing new added. It shows what happens anyway, so you can compare the others with it.
quiz.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

quiz.p: In Spice Guard, you count the same 16 grid squares on each potato, every day. Why?
opts: So the numbers on each potato and each day can be compared fairly
quiz.why: Counting the same squares on every potato, on the same days, makes the numbers comparable.
quiz.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

quiz.p: Which medicine for high blood pressure came from sarpagandha root?
quiz.why: Reserpine was taken out of sarpagandha root in 1952. Aspirin came from a chemical in willow bark, and artemisinin from sweet wormwood.

quiz.p: Asima Chatterjee helped make Ayush-56, a medicine for epilepsy. Which plant did Ayush-56 come from?
opts: A small water fern, Marsilea minuta
quiz.why: Asima Chatterjee studied Marsilea minuta, a water fern eaten in Bengal as sushni shak.

quiz.p: A fair trial of a remedy gives one group the remedy. What does the control group get?
opts: A placebo that looks and tastes the same but should do nothing
Nothing, and they are told so
quiz.why: A placebo stops people knowing which group they are in, because believing you got a remedy can make you feel better.

quiz.p: Why can a natural plant oil, like clove oil, be dangerous for a small child?
opts: Defence chemicals are strong, and a large dose can poison
Clove oil is made in a factory
quiz.why: The dose decides. A drop on a tooth can help. A spoonful swallowed by a child can harm badly.

quiz.p: Which plant is endemic to India, growing wild nowhere else?
quiz.why: Red sanders grows wild only in the southern Eastern Ghats. Gulmohar is from Madagascar and eucalyptus from Australia.

quiz.p: Tamarind is used in rasam all over South India. Where did tamarind first grow?
quiz.why: Tamarind first grew in Africa and reached India long ago.

quiz.p: A farmer plants pieces of sugarcane to grow a new field. Why must each piece have a node?
opts: New shoots and roots grow from the nodes
The pieces are easier to carry
quiz.why: A node holds the bud for a new shoot and can grow roots. A piece of cane with no node cannot grow into a new plant.

quiz.p: Two pots of the same size hold the same soil and stand side by side on a balcony. One is clay and one is plastic. Which will need water more often?
opts: The clay pot, because water slowly escapes through the clay
The plastic pot, because plastic is thin
Both need water at exactly the same times
quiz.why: Water slowly escapes through the walls of a clay pot as well as from the soil surface. So a clay pot dries out faster, and the finger test matters even more.

quiz.p: Why was the 1995 patent on using turmeric for wounds cancelled?
opts: Old Indian texts showed the use was already known
Turmeric does not grow in America
quiz.why: You cannot patent something that people already knew and used. India's scientists showed the old texts.

open_questions.q: How do neelakurinji and muli bamboo count the years before they flower?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found the clock inside these plants, or how all the plants of one kind flower together.

open_questions.q: Does haldi, taken as food or medicine, really help any illness in people?
open_questions.why_open: Thousands of laboratory studies exist, but no large fair trial has yet settled it. Scientists still argue about how much curcumin the body takes in.

open_questions.q: How many of India's plants hold medicines that nobody has found yet?
open_questions.why_open: Only a small part of India's plants has been tested carefully. Many healers' knowledge has never been written down.

open_questions.q: Who should own traditional plant knowledge, and how should the money be shared?
open_questions.why_open: Countries, communities and companies still argue about this. India's laws and international agreements try to answer it, and cases are still being decided.

open_questions.q: What do plants experience when they are bitten?
open_questions.why_open: We can measure the signals a plant sends. What the plant feels, and how to study that, is still argued about.

open_questions.q: How many of India's endemic plants are in danger?
open_questions.why_open: Many plants have never been counted properly in the wild, so scientists do not know how many are disappearing.

maths.problem: In Spice Guard, Revathi, a girl in Class 4 in Kochi, found that her plain potato had 12 mouldy squares out of 16 on day 6. What fraction of the potato was mouldy? Write it in its simplest form.
maths.answer: 12 out of 16, which is three quarters.
maths.explain: 12 out of 16 is 12/16. Both numbers divide by 4. 12 divided by 4 is 3, and 16 divided by 4 is 4. So 12/16 is the same as 3/4, three quarters of the potato.
maths.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how much of the whole potato was mouldy, so potatoes of different sizes could still be compared.

maths.problem: The plain potato in Spice Guard had these mouldy squares: day 2: 0, day 3: 1, day 4: 3, day 5: 7, day 6: 12. Between which two days did the mould spread the most? Predict roughly how many squares would be mouldy on day 7.
maths.answer: Between day 5 and day 6, when 5 more squares went mouldy. On day 7, probably all 16 or close to it.
maths.explain: Find each change: 0 to 1 is 1, 1 to 3 is 2, 3 to 7 is 4, 7 to 12 is 5. The biggest jump is 5, between day 5 and day 6. The jumps are getting bigger, so the next jump could be more than 5. 12 + 5 is 17, but there are only 16 squares, so about 16.
maths.context: In Spice Guard, you put four potato squares in closed boxes: one plain, one with rice flour, one with haldi and one with clove powder. Then you counted mould for a week.

chart.title: Plain potato: mouldy squares each day

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows the speed of change. A line that gets steeper shows mould spreading faster each day, which helps us predict.

maths.problem: In the Node Test, the longest root on cutting A was 6 mm on day 7 and 34 mm on day 14. About how many millimetres did the root grow each day in that week?
maths.explain: 34 take away 6 is 28 mm of growth. That happened in 7 days, from day 7 to day 14. 28 divided by 7 is 4. So the root grew about 4 mm each day.
maths.context: In the Node Test, you stood three money plant cuttings in water: one with a node and a leaf, one with a node and no leaf, and one with no node.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the growth by the number of days gives a growth rate, so we can compare roots measured on different days.

maths.problem: In Holiday Water, Ritu, a girl in Class 4, built a wick design. It used 120 ml of water a day from a bottle that holds 1 litre. A litre is 1,000 ml. Will the bottle last for a 7-day trip?
maths.answer: Yes. 7 days need 840 ml, and the bottle holds 1,000 ml, so 160 ml would be left.
maths.explain: 7 times 120 is 840 ml for the whole trip. 1,000 take away 840 is 160. The bottle has enough, with 160 ml to spare.
maths.context: In Holiday Water, you designed a way to keep a pot plant watered for a week while nobody is home.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the daily use by the number of days tells us before the trip whether the design will work.

maths.problem: Neelakurinji covered the hills of Munnar in blue in 2018. They bloom about every 12 years. In which years after that would you expect the next two big blooms?
maths.explain: 2018 + 12 is 2030. 2030 + 12 is 2042. The pattern adds 12 each time. Real blooms can be a year early or late.
maths.why_maths: A repeating gap in time is a number pattern, so we can predict when a rare bloom will come again.

maths.problem: Muli bamboo in Mizoram flowered in 1959 and again from 2006 to 2008, about every 48 years. Starting from 1959, add 48 years. Is the answer inside 2006 to 2008? Then predict the next flowering.
maths.answer: 1959 + 48 is 2007, which is inside 2006 to 2008. The next flowering would be around 2055.
maths.why_maths: Adding the gap checks whether the pattern really fits the past, before we use it to predict the future.

maths.problem: In Ask the Elders, Sunita, a girl in Class 4, collected 10 family plant remedies. 2 had been tested in fair trials and found to work. 1 had been tested and did not work. The rest had not been tested fairly yet. How many had not been tested? What fraction of all the remedies is that?
maths.answer: 7 had not been tested. That is 7 out of 10, or seven tenths.
maths.explain: 2 + 1 is 3 tested. 10 take away 3 is 7 not tested. 7 out of 10 is 7/10.
maths.context: In Ask the Elders, you collected your family's plant remedies and marked how sure we are about each one.
maths.why_maths: Counting and a bar chart show at a glance how much of what we know is tested, and how much is still a question.

maths.problem: In a trial of a cold remedy, 14 of 20 people who took the remedy were better in 5 days. 13 of 20 people who took a placebo were better in 5 days. Mohan, a boy in Class 4, says the remedy works because 14 is more than 13. What would you tell him?
maths.answer: The difference is only 1 person out of 20. That could easily be luck. The trial does not show that the remedy works.
maths.explain: 14 out of 20 and 13 out of 20 are very close: 70 out of every 100 and 65 out of every 100. If the trial were done again, the numbers could easily swap. A real effect would need a bigger, clearer difference, or many more people.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers is not enough. We have to ask whether a small difference could have happened by chance.

how_we_found_out.context: How did an Indian village remedy become one of the world's first medicines for high blood pressure? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For centuries, healers in India used the root of sarpagandha, Indian snakeroot, to calm people who were very anxious or unwell in their minds, and for fevers and snakebite. Doctors trained in Europe mostly treated this as village folklore. In 1931, two doctors in Kolkata, G. Sen and K. C. Bose, reported that the root lowered blood pressure. The same year, the chemists Salimuzzaman Siddiqui and Rafat Husain Siddiqui took several new chemicals out of the root. Few doctors abroad paid attention. In 1949, the Mumbai heart doctor Rustom Jal Vakil published a careful study of patients in the British Heart Journal. Now the world listened. In 1952, chemists at a Swiss company took out the root's most powerful chemical and named it reserpine. Within a few years, reserpine was used around the world for high blood pressure. Later, doctors found it could cause sadness and tiredness in some people, so newer medicines replaced it. But it showed that a village remedy could be tested fairly, and be right.
how_we_found_out.who: G. Sen and K. C. Bose, doctors in Kolkata; Salimuzzaman Siddiqui and Rafat Husain Siddiqui, chemists; Rustom Jal Vakil, a heart doctor in Mumbai; chemists at a Swiss company who named reserpine
how_we_found_out.when: 1931 (first reports), 1949 (Vakil's study), 1952 (reserpine taken out of the root)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That village plant remedies from India were folklore not worth testing. Careful studies by Indian doctors and chemists showed that sarpagandha really lowers blood pressure.
how_we_found_out.art: A sarpagandha plant with small white-pink flowers and a twisted root, next to an old journal page and a blood pressure cuff.

playtest: Walked through every part as a parent and child in a city flat would. Plant Shields: the card backs were printed with the answer and the fronts were numbered in pairs, so the game could be won without remembering anything; fronts now carry no numbers, the shield card names its plant, and the backs say only Plant or Shield. Fair Test Judge: a made-up child with the same name as the story's brother was renamed, and the 2-player rule (the reader does not judge their own card, and the job swaps each card) is written out. Spice Guard: step minutes, the schedule and the total now agree, and a name-free kid question was fixed. Node Test: the node was about 4 cm above the water in pieces A and B, so no roots could grow where the node was dry; pieces are now about 3 cm with the node in the water. Too Much Water?: 30 ml a day would have overflowed a paper cup in three days, so it is now 20 ml in plastic cups on saucers, with what to do if cup C fills, and the schedule lists every day. Herb pot: lemongrass waits for roots before planting. Pressing: how to stop mould in humid weather. Worksheets and quiz: removed the repeats (rice flour, no-node, soggy tulsi) and replaced them with new questions (repeating a test, clay against plastic pot, sugarcane, invasive plants); names in questions are now introduced; one result was made a plain 'suppose'. Two jokes were not funny and were replaced. The three videos have no checked address yet; I could not open them. Facts were read against the sources list.
